legacy_report:
SOURCE: "DuckDB: an Embeddable Analytical Database", Mark Raasveldt and Hannes Mühleisen (CWI, Amsterdam). SIGMOD '19, June 30-July 5, 2019, Amsterdam. ACM, 4 pages, doi 10.1145/3299869.3320212. The page headers are marked "Demonstration", so this is the demo track.

COVERAGE: 20572 of 20572 chars read, all 4 pages (pp. 1981-1984). Nothing skipped. The extraction is clean text.

VERDICT ON THE NOTE'S WORDING
- "SQLite for analytics": NOT in the paper as a phrase. The nearest text is the abstract: "The immense popularity of SQLite shows that there is a need for unobtrusive in-process data management solutions. However, there is no such system yet geared towards analytical workloads." Do not present "SQLite for analytics" as a quotation from the authors. The paper does position DuckDB as the analytical counterpart to SQLite, so "analytical counterpart to SQLite" is accurate. "In-process" and "embedded" are in the paper.
- "In-process OLAP engine": supported. See the first claim below.
- Vectorised execution: in the paper. It is described as a vectorized interpreted engine, not a columnar one. The paper never uses "columnar" for the execution engine.
- "Columnar": only indirect. Storage is described as "chunks of columns" compressed into blocks (DataBlocks). It is not stated as a columnar engine.
- Parquet: ZERO mentions. The paper does not say DuckDB queries Parquet. It does not mention CSV either. A search of the extracted text finds no "Parquet" and no "CSV". That claim needs a different source, such as DuckDB docs. Do not cite this paper for it.
- Venue: confirmed as SIGMOD '19 (demonstration paper).

CLAIMS
- claim: DuckDB is an embedded (in-process) analytical SQL database, built because SQLite does not serve analytical workloads.
  number: none
  setup: design and positioning statement.
  quote: "We demonstrate DuckDB, a novel data management system designed to execute analytical SQL queries while embedded in another process."
  where: p.1 abstract
- claim: SQLite is OLTP-focused with a row-major engine on a B-Tree, so its OLAP performance is "very poor". The paper gives no benchmark for this.
  number: "more than a trillion databases" (SQLite deployment, cited to the SQLite website, [4])
  setup: motivation in the introduction.
  quote: "SQLite strongly focuses on transactional (OLTP) workloads, and contains a row-major execution engine operating on a B-Tree storage format [3]. As a consequence, SQLite's performance on analytical (OLAP) workloads is very poor." Earlier in the same paragraph: "the most widely deployed SQL database engine with more than a trillion databases in active use [4]".
  where: p.1
- claim: The execution engine is vectorized and interpreted, not JIT-compiled. The authors chose this for portability, because JIT depends on large compiler libraries.
  number: 1024 values per vector by default
  setup: design section.
  quote: "DuckDB uses a vectorized interpreted execution engine [1]. This approach was chosen over Just-in-Time compilation (JIT) of SQL queries [8] for portability reasons. JIT engines depend on massive compiler libraries (e.g. LLVM) with additional transitive dependencies. DuckDB uses vectors of a fixed maximum amount of values (1024 per default)."
  where: p.3
- claim: Execution follows a "Vector Volcano" pull model. The root pulls chunks from child nodes until a scan operator produces them, and a chunk is a horizontal subset of a result set, intermediate or base table.
  number: none
  setup: design section.
  quote: "The execution engine executes the query in a so-called \"Vector Volcano\"model. Query execution commences by pulling the first \"chunk\" of data from the root node of the physical plan."
  where: p.3
- claim: Vector layout: fixed-length types are native arrays, strings are pointers into a string heap, NULLs sit in a separate bit vector, and selection vectors avoid shifting data after a filter.
  number: none
  setup: design section.
  quote: "Fixed-length types such as integers are stored as native arrays. Variable-length values such as strings are represented as a native array of pointers into a separate string heap. NULL values are represented using a separate bit vector"
  where: p.3
- claim: Component stack. The paper says no component is new; the authors combined state-of-the-art methods.
  number: none
  setup: Table 1.
  quote: "API C/C++/SQLite; SQL Parser libpg_query [2]; Optimizer Cost-Based [7, 9]; Execution Engine Vectorized [1]; Concurrency Control Serializable MVCC [10]; Storage DataBlocks [5]". Also: "none of DuckDB's components is revolutionary in its own regard. Instead, we combined methods and algorithms from the state of the art that were best suited for our use cases."
  where: pp.2-3
- claim: Storage is a read-optimized layout with columns compressed in horizontally partitioned blocks. Each block carries min/max indexes per column.
  number: none
  setup: the DataBlocks design from Lang et al. 2016. The paper's next-steps section says DataBlocks is not yet complete.
  quote: "DuckDB uses the read-optimized DataBlocks storage layout [5]. Logical tables are horizontally partitioned into chunks of columns which are compressed into physical blocks using light-weight compression methods. Blocks carry min/max indexes for every column"
  where: p.3
- claim: ACID comes from HyPer's serializable MVCC. Updates are made in place, with old versions kept in an undo buffer. MVCC was chosen because parallel table modification was often requested.
  number: none
  setup: design section.
  quote: "This variant updates data in-place immediately, and keeps previous states stored in a separate undo buffer for concurrent transactions and aborts."
  where: p.3
- claim: Four requirements for embedded analytical databases: efficient OLAP without sacrificing all OLTP, fast table transfer in the same address space, stability (never crash the host), and portability with no external dependencies.
  number: none
  setup: lessons from MonetDBLite.
  quote: "High degree of stability, if the embedded database crashes, for example due to an out-of-memory situation, it takes the host down with it. This can never happen."
  where: p.2
- claim: Current state. DuckDB passes all TPC-H and all but two TPC-DS queries, and most of SQLite's logic test suite. The authors expected full TPC-DS by the time of the demo.
  number: all TPC-H, all but 2 TPC-DS queries, "millions" of test queries
  setup: status at writing, 2019.
  quote: "As of this writing, DuckDB runs all TPC-H queries and all but two TPC-DS queries." and "DuckDB also already completes most of SQLite's SQL logic test suite that contains millions of queries."
  where: p.4
- claim: Interface. DuckDB has a C/C++ API, a SQLite compatibility layer (re-linking or library overloading), and R (DBI) and Python (PEP 249) APIs. It is MIT-licensed.
  number: none
  setup: design section.
  quote: "DuckDB provides a SQLite compatibility layer, allowing applications that previously used SQLite to use DuckDB through re-linking or library overloading." Also "DuckDB is available as Open-Source software under the permissive MIT license".
  where: pp.2-3
- claim: Use cases named are interactive analysis in R/Python (dplyr, Pandas) and edge computing (power meters analysed on the node, to avoid bandwidth and privacy problems).
  number: none
  setup: motivation.
  quote: "connected power meters currently forward data to a central location for analysis. This is problematic due to bandwidth limitations especially on radio interfaces, and also raises pri-vacy concerns."
  where: p.2

LIMITS
- There are NO performance numbers. It is a demo proposal. The comparison is a live demo against SQLite, MonetDBLite and HyPer on TPC-H. The only performance claims are predictions, for example "only DuckDB will be able to continue functioning for larger ones".
- The authors concede the system is incomplete. Quote: "Immediate next steps for DuckDB are completion of DataBlocks storage scheme and cardinality estimating. A buffer manager is also not yet implemented, but will be. DuckDB already supports inter-query parallelism but intra-query parallelism will be added as well."
- Self-checking and checksums are only future ideas.
- The paper says nothing on Parquet, CSV, extensions, larger-than-memory operation, or the "SQLite for analytics" tagline. Later DuckDB features are not in this paper, so the note cannot cite it for them.
- The paper claims "no purpose-built embeddable analytical database" existed, and MonetDBLite is the authors' own prior system.

BUILDS ON (as printed)
- Boncz, Zukowski, Nes 2005, MonetDB/X100 (vectorized execution).
- Neumann, Mühlbauer, Kemper 2015 (serializable MVCC).
- Lang et al. 2016, Data Blocks.
- Moerkotte and Neumann 2008 (dynamic programming join ordering).
- Neumann and Kemper 2015 (unnesting subqueries).
- Neumann and Radke 2018 (greedy fallback for large joins).
- Fittl 2019, libpg_query (Postgres parser).
- Raasveldt and Mühleisen 2018, MonetDBLite.
- Raasveldt and Mühleisen 2017, "Don't Hold My Data Hostage" (client protocol).
- Neumann 2011 (JIT compilation, the approach DuckDB rejects).

CODE: none.

FIGURES
- Fig 1 "Systems Landscape", p.2: a 2x2 grid of OLTP/OLAP against embedded/stand-alone. The embedded-OLAP cell is marked "?" and that is the gap DuckDB fills. It is the quickest way to explain the positioning.
- Fig 2 "Demonstration setup schematic", p.3: the four machines (SQLite, MonetDBLite, HyPer, DuckDB) with a dataset-size dial and live metrics. Not run through the figure script.
- Table 1 "DuckDB: Component Overview", p.2: see the component-stack claim above.

PROBLEMS: None. The extraction is clean and there are no embedded instructions. The text has minor hyphenation artefacts ("pri-vacy"), which I kept in quotes verbatim.
